record.paper_title: Solving Open Problems in Right Alternative Rings with Z-Module Reasoning
record.original_question: Let R be a right alternative ring, meaning a possibly nonassociative ring in which x(yy) = xyy for all x and y. If the associator is defined by (x, y, z) = (xy)z - x(yz), is it always true that for every x, y in R one has ((x, x, y)(x, x, y))x((x, x, y)(x, x, y)) = 0? Equivalently, must (x, x, y)^2 x (x, x, y)^2 vanish identically in every right alternative ring?

evidence.quote: 3. A computer solution of the open problem: for all x, y in a right alternative ring, (x, x, y)2x(x, x, y)2 = 0.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A right alternative ring is a (not necessarily associative) ring R satisfying the identity x(yy) = (xy)y for all x, y in R. Define the associator of three elements by (x, y, z) := (xy)z - x(yz). Prove or disprove: for every right alternative ring R and all x, y in R,
   (x, x, y)^2 · x · (x, x, y)^2 = 0,
where (x, x, y)^2 denotes the square (x, x, y)(x, x, y) in R. Equivalently, show that the identity ((x,x,y)(x,x,y)) x ((x,x,y)(x,x,y)) = 0 holds in every right alternative ring.
artifact.status_search_result: The identity (x,x,y)^2 x (x,x,y)^2 = 0 in right alternative rings was established as a theorem via automated/computer-assisted reasoning (Z-module reasoning). It is reported as proved in the literature on automated theorem proving applied to nonassociative rings.

status_evidence.claim: The identity has been established as a theorem by automated reasoning.
